prints.title: The Herdsman
prints.desc: Before the sun comes up, he's already moving. By the time most people hit snooze for the third time, he's already made a hundred small decisions. Already read the sky, already checked the ground, already done the quiet math of a man who knows his animals and his land better than he knows anything else. This is not a job he clocked into. This is a life he was shaped for. And there's something in the way he carries himself, something unhurried and sure, that makes you stop and wonder if maybe the rest of us have been moving too fast all along

prints.title: Reach
prints.desc:
I know this girl. Her name is Abena, and she's always been curious about everything. I'd photographed her once before, so when I saw her again on a Sunday afternoon while walking home from church, I took my phone out and started taking pictures. She was used to it by then and didn't mind.

When I finished, she reached for the phone. She wanted to see the photos I'd just taken of her. That's it, really. That's the whole moment. But it stuck with me. A young girl wanting to see herself, wanting to know what I saw when I photographed her. It felt like more than curiosity. It felt like she was asking to be included, not just photographed.

This photo is that reach. Nothing posed, nothing staged. Just Abena, wanting to see.

prints.title: The Purple Market
prints.desc:
I had gone to Dome market for fish, and a few other things for the week. Nothing about the afternoon was unusual. I got what I needed and was on my way out when these two women walked past me, quickly, the way people move when they are already thinking about the next job.

They are 'Kayayei'. Women who carry other people's loads for a living, moving through markets like these ones, offering their backs to whoever needs help getting home. I have seen them for years and never stopped to really look. This time I did. There is an art in how they carry themselves. Not effortless. Nothing about that work is effortless, but practiced. Purposeful. Unbothered. Like the weight is just something they made peace with a long time ago. You see it in the posture, in the pace, in how little of it shows on the face.

The light was doing something specific that afternoon, low and warm, catching them from the side in a way I could not have arranged if I had tried. I lifted my phone before I could think about it. That is usually when the photograph works.

The load carried without complaint. The body as a record of what has been asked of it.
